extracted.intended_audience: registered patent and trademark practitioners before the USPTO (practitioners/attorneys of record)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and obligations for practitioners representing foreign‑domiciled trademark applicants before the USPTO, including required procedures, certification duties, supervision of non‑practitioners, and consequences for violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (representation requirement for foreign‑domiciled applicants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants, registrants, or parties to a trademark proceeding whose domicile is not located within the U.S. or its territories must be represented by an attorney who is an active member in good standing of the bar of the highest court of a state in the U.S. (Requirement of U.S. Licensed Attorney for Foreign Trademark Applicants and Registrants, 84 Fed. Reg. 31498). See 37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Became effective August 3, 2019. Intended to increase compliance with U.S. trademark law, improve accuracy of submissions, and safeguard the integrity of the U.S. trademark register by preventing unauthorized practice. Practitioners representing foreign‑domiciled applicants are expected to be reasonably well informed about the rule and its implications (e.g., bona fide review of specimens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specimen requirement for §1(a) applications (use in commerce)
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark application filed under section 1(a) of the Trademark Act must include a specimen that shows the mark as used in commerce. In signing a section 1(a) application, the practitioner declares that the specimen shows the mark as used in commerce (signed under penalty of perjury).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mock-ups or digitally altered specimens are not proper specimens because they do not demonstrate use in commerce (see TMEP §§ 904.03(a), 904.04; TMEP § 904.04(a)(i)). False statements are subject to 18 U.S.C. § 1001. The signatory represents that statements of their own knowledge are true and statements made on information and belief are believed to be true (37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certifications upon presentation of papers (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: By presenting any paper to the USPTO, the presenter certifies that (a) statements of the party's own knowledge are true, statements on information and belief are believed to be true, and that willful falsification is subject to criminal penalties, and (b) to the best of the party's knowledge, information and belief, formed after a reasonable inquiry, factual allegations have evidentiary support or are likely to after investigation and denials are warranted on the evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations may be subject to penalties under 18 U.S.C. § 1001 and jeopardize the probative value of the paper. The rule requires an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances before certifying factual statements or the adequacy of evidentiary support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation to a client (37 C.F.R. § 11.101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes managing workload so the practitioner can devote sufficient time to review filings, putting procedures in place to ensure compliance with USPTO regulations, and having systems (e.g., conflict checks) to manage client matters. Accepting volumes of work such that adequate review cannot be provided constitutes a failure of competence (document example: reviewing 2½–10 minutes per application and handling tens of thousands of matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client (37 C.F.R. § 11.103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to devote sufficient time to client matters, failing to institute procedures to ensure compliance with USPTO regulations, and failing to adequately review trademark applications (including specimens to confirm actual use in commerce) violate this duty. Examples of inadequate practice include rushed or sloppy reviews and overreliance on non‑practitioner reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision and compatibility of non‑practitioners' conduct (37 C.F.R. § 11.503)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall take reasonable efforts to ensure that non‑practitioners' conduct is compatible with the professional obligations of the practitioner (37 C.F.R. § 11.503).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must properly review and vet documents prepared or reviewed by non‑practitioner assistants before signing and filing. Allowing non‑practitioners to prepare/file trademark documents without adequate practitioner oversight is a breach (document notes the respondent allowed a non‑practitioner assistant to review many applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Not assisting unauthorized practice of law (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not assist another in practicing law in a jurisdiction in violation of the regulation of the legal profession in that jurisdiction (37 C.F.R. § 11.505).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing non‑practitioners to prepare and file trademark documents on behalf of clients without proper review or vetting may assist unauthorized practice and violates this rule. Practitioners must ensure their actions do not facilitate non‑practitioners acting as attorneys.

rubrics_metrics.name: No misrepresentation; avoid conduct prejudicial to USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) & (d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in misrepresentation (11.804(c)) or conduct prejudicial to the administration of the USPTO trademark registration process (11.804(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signing declarations attesting to use in commerce or specimen authenticity without performing a reasonable inquiry violates these provisions. Misrepresentations undermine the integrity of the trademark register; digitally created or altered specimens are examples of problematic submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid other conduct reflecting adversely on fitness (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office in trademark matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision covers conduct not specifically enumerated elsewhere but that nonetheless reflects poorly on fitness; the Office may treat such conduct as disciplinary even if it does not neatly fit other rule violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict‑of‑interest procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must have a system to check for conflicts of interest before taking or signing matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of any conflict check system is a deficiency; the respondent initially lacked one and later implemented a conflict check database. Implementing and using conflict‑checking procedures is part of competent representation and professional responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit caseload to ensure quality representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners should limit the volume of incoming trademark work to ensure they can provide clients with quality representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting an excessive volume (document example: attorney of record on over 32,000 applications and >400 filed in one day) without systems to ensure review and supervision demonstrates failure to provide competent and diligent representation. Practitioners should reasonably control intake and staffing to permit adequate review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision of signature and review practices (E‑sign usage and signing declarations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using electronic signature methods, practitioners remain responsible for reviewing the application before signing and filing, including any submissions reviewed by non‑practitioner assistants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the attorney personally signs via electronic methods (e.g., USPTO E‑SIGN ON link), the attorney must ensure a reasonable inquiry was performed into the truth of declarations (e.g., use in commerce). Reliance on an assistant's review without independent verification is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation with OED investigations and ongoing obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent shall cooperate fully with the USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline in present or future USPTO inquiries related to improper filings by trademark entities with whom the respondent works or had worked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation may be a mitigating factor but also a continuing obligation; failure to cooperate can lead to further discipline. The Final Order required cooperation and noted respondent's cooperation as a consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for reinstatement and remedial requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of reinstatement after suspension, the respondent must meet specified requirements (e.g., provide sworn affidavit and evidence of completion of six (6) hours of CLE on ethics/professional responsibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent may petition for reinstatement at 18 months but OED will not grant until after the full suspension period; petitioners must comply with 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58 and 11.60 (with specified modifications) and may be placed on probation after reinstatement. Failure to comply during probation can trigger further suspension procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal and client notification obligations upon suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: Within sixty (60) days from the date of the Final Order, the respondent shall withdraw from representation in all matters pending before the Office and provide all clients having immediate or prospective business before the Office written notice of the suspension and a copy of the Final Order translated into the client's native language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For clients outside Japan, electronic communication is permitted if (i) respondent maintains a record of notices and (ii) the electronic service provides delivery receipts or the respondent obtains written confirmation from the client. Within seventy‑five (75) days the respondent must file an affidavit of compliance with the OED Director certifying full compliance with the Final Order and the cited withdrawal procedures (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.116).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public posting and future use of disciplinary record
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director shall electronically publish the Final Order in the OED FOIA Reading Room and publish a notice in the Official Gazette; the Office may consider the disciplinary record in future proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing prevents the Office from considering the record of this proceeding when addressing further complaints or as an aggravating factor in future discipline, to rebut statements by respondent, or in connection with requests for reconsideration under 37 C.F.R. § 11.60. Disciplinary decisions are public and can affect future matters involving the practitioner.
